title: Questions and sources, exercise class VIII — norm production, codification, the Historical School

1.title: The sources of norm production, with an example of each
1.text: The question calls for A LIST WITH EXAMPLES, not merely for names. (1) THE STATUTE (legislation) — a general norm issued for the future by the organ competent to do so; examples: the ABGB (1811), the Code civil (1804), the BGB (1900). Within it degrees are distinguished: CONSTITUTION, STATUTE, REGULATION. (2) CUSTOM (customary law) — a long-standing practice (LONGA CONSUETUDO) coupled with the conviction that it is binding (OPINIO IURIS); examples: the French COUTUMES, the German Weistümer, and to this day mercantile custom and, in international law, custom as a fully-fledged source. (3) JUDICIAL DECISION (case law, precedent) — in the common law A SOURCE OF LAW in the proper sense, binding under STARE DECISIS (Donoghue v Stevenson, Marbury v Madison); on the continent formally not a source, but in fact one, especially in the supreme and constitutional courts. (4) LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP (doctrine) — in Rome the RESPONSA of the jurists, in the Middle Ages the GLOSSA ORDINARIA ('what the gloss does not recognize, the court does not recognize'), among the Pandectists a systematics that was then embodied in the BGB; today it is no longer a source, but it interprets and prepares. (5) THE TREATY — as a source of objective law above all in international law (the Peace of Westphalia 1648, the Treaty of Versailles 1919, the Treaties of Rome 1957), but also the COLLECTIVE AGREEMENT in labour law. (6) PRIVILEGE AND THE INDIVIDUAL ACT OF THE RULER — a common source in the Middle Ages and the early modern period (the Privilegium minus 1156, the Golden Bull 1356). (7) A RELIGIOUS TEXT AND ITS INTERPRETATION — the Torah and the Talmud, the Qur'an and the Sunna, canon law. (8) NATURAL LAW — a source of its own kind, serving as a standard and a source of arguments (Art. 16 of the Declaration of 1789, § 16 ABGB, today ius cogens and human rights). THE POINT TO TAKE AWAY: WHICH SOURCE IS THE PRINCIPAL ONE CHANGES THROUGH HISTORY — in the Middle Ages custom and judicial finding, in the early modern period learned doctrine, from the codifications the statute, and in the 20th century judicial decision grows stronger; that shift is precisely the axis of this whole course.

terms.def: The two conditions of custom: a long-standing practice and the conviction that it is binding.

cards.q: What are the sources of norm production? Give an example of each.
cards.a: THE STATUTE (ABGB 1811, Code civil 1804, BGB 1900); CUSTOM (the French coutumes, mercantile custom, international custom) requiring LONGA CONSUETUDO + OPINIO IURIS; JUDICIAL DECISION (stare decisis, Marbury v Madison); LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP (the Roman responsa, the Glossa ordinaria, Pandectism); THE TREATY (the Peace of Westphalia, Versailles, the Treaties of Rome, the collective agreement); PRIVILEGE (the Golden Bull 1356); A RELIGIOUS TEXT; NATURAL LAW.

cards.q: How did the principal source of law change through history?
cards.a: In the MIDDLE AGES custom and judicial finding; in the EARLY MODERN PERIOD learned doctrine (the ius commune); FROM THE CODIFICATIONS the statute; and in the 20TH CENTURY JUDICIAL DECISION grows stronger. That shift is precisely the axis of the whole course.

2.title: The first codifications of private law and what was new about them
2.text: THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: the second half of the 18th and the beginning of the 19th century, that is, the ENLIGHTENMENT, RATIONAL NATURAL LAW AND ENLIGHTENED ABSOLUTISM. The ruler wants a UNIFORM, SURVEYABLE AND RATIONAL ORDER for the whole territory — partly in order to be able to administer a growing state, partly because he believes that reason can derive such an order. THE REGIONS: central and continental Europe — BAVARIA (the Codex Maximilianeus Bavaricus Civilis, 1756), PRUSSIA (the Allgemeines Landrecht, 1794), FRANCE (the Code civil, 1804), AUSTRIA (the ABGB, 1811). England avoided codification. WHAT WAS FUNDAMENTALLY NEW BY COMPARISON WITH PREVIOUS LEGISLATIVE TECHNIQUE — and this is the core of the question: (1) COMPLETENESS — the code aims to regulate THE WHOLE FIELD, not individual cases; it is to have no gaps. (2) EXCLUSIVITY — it DEROGATES ALL EXISTING LAW in that field, including custom and the ius commune; henceforth only the code applies. (3) SYSTEMATIC CHARACTER — the material is arranged according to a logical plan (the institutional or the Pandectist system), not in a random order of cases. (4) ABSTRACTNESS AND GENERALITY — the norms are written as general rules, not casuistically as 'if — then'. (5) PERSONAL AND TERRITORIAL UNIFORMITY — it applies to ALL INHABITANTS of the territory regardless of estate, thereby breaking up estate-based and particular law. (6) INTELLIGIBILITY — it is to be readable even by the uneducated, because law is to be knowable (hence also the language: the ABGB is in German, not Latin). WHY EUROPEAN-STYLE CODIFICATIONS ACQUIRED SUCH INFLUENCE OUTSIDE EUROPE IN THE 19TH AND 20TH CENTURIES: (a) COLONIAL IMPOSITION in directly ruled territories; (b) FORCED 'OPENING' and the effort to be rid of the CAPITULATIONS and consular jurisdiction — Japan, the Ottoman Empire, Egypt and Siam adopted European codes in order to prove their 'civilization' and obtain the abolition of foreigners' privileges; (c) a MODERNIZING CHOICE by local elites, for whom a code was an instrument of unification and state-building (Turkey adopts the Swiss ZGB in 1926); (d) PRESTIGE AND PRACTICALITY — a ready-made, tested text is easier to take over than a centuries-long development of one's own; (e) THE NEEDS OF THE WORLD MARKET, which requires intelligible contract and property law.

cards.q: In what context and where did the first codifications of private law arise?
cards.a: The second half of the 18th and the beginning of the 19th century: the ENLIGHTENMENT, RATIONAL NATURAL LAW AND ENLIGHTENED ABSOLUTISM — the ruler wants a UNIFORM, SURVEYABLE AND RATIONAL ORDER for the whole territory. The regions: BAVARIA (the Codex Maximilianeus 1756), PRUSSIA (the ALR 1794), FRANCE (the Code civil 1804), AUSTRIA (the ABGB 1811). England avoided codification.

cards.q: What was fundamentally new about codification by comparison with previous technique? Six points.
cards.a: 1) COMPLETENESS — to regulate THE WHOLE FIELD without gaps. 2) EXCLUSIVITY — it DEROGATES all existing law including custom and the ius commune. 3) SYSTEMATIC CHARACTER on a logical plan. 4) ABSTRACTNESS — general rules instead of casuistry. 5) PERSONAL AND TERRITORIAL UNIFORMITY — for everyone regardless of estate. 6) INTELLIGIBILITY, because law is to be knowable (hence German, not Latin).

cards.q: Why did European codifications acquire such influence outside Europe?
cards.a: 1) COLONIAL IMPOSITION. 2) The effort to be rid of the CAPITULATIONS and consular jurisdiction — Japan, the Ottoman Empire, Egypt and Siam adopted codes in order to prove their 'civilization'. 3) A MODERNIZING CHOICE by local elites (Turkey adopts the Swiss ZGB in 1926). 4) PRESTIGE AND PRACTICALITY — a ready-made text is easier to take over than a development of one's own. 5) THE NEEDS OF THE WORLD MARKET.

3.title: Source: § 16 ABGB — innate rights
3.text: THE SOURCE: '§ 16: Every human being has innate rights, already knowable by reason, and is therefore to be regarded as a person. Slavery or serfdom and the exercise of power relating thereto are not permitted in these lands.' THE EUROPEAN CONTEXT: this is a text of 1811, that is, after the French Revolution and during the Napoleonic wars. The sentence about innate rights knowable by REASON is purely natural-law and belongs to the same family as the American Declaration of Independence (1776) and the French Declaration (1789). THE AUSTRIAN CONTEXT AND THE ROAD TO THE ABGB: (1) MARIA THERESA sets up a COMPILATION COMMISSION in 1753, whose fruit is the CODEX THERESIANUS (1766) — too voluminous, casuistic and estate-based, and therefore not adopted. (2) JOSEPH II issues the JOSEPHINE CODE in 1786, but only its first part (the law of persons) — it contains, among other things, the removal of estate distinctions in private law and civil marriage. (3) THE ABOLITION OF SERFDOM by the patent of 1781 is the material precondition of § 16. (4) The work continues under Leopold II and Francis II; the commission is led by KARL ANTON VON MARTINI and after him by FRANZ VON ZEILLER, a pupil of Kant and the actual author of the final form. (5) THE TRIAL RUN: the West Galician Code (1797) was tried out in the newly acquired territories and, after revision, became the basis. (6) ON 1 JUNE 1811 the ABGB is promulgated, in force from 1 January 1812, for the GERMAN HEREDITARY LANDS (not, therefore, for Hungary). THE HOPES INVESTED IN THAT SENTENCE: equality of all before private law regardless of estate and denomination; the legal personality of every human being as a PERSON, that is, the prohibition of treating a human being as a thing; the definitive end of personal unfreedom; and the idea that law can be derived from reason and made universal. THE BACKGROUND: the Enlightenment, Kant's philosophy of autonomy (Zeiller was a Kantian), the abolition of serfdom and the atmosphere after the revolution. THE FEARS SUCH A SENTENCE AROUSED IN POSITIVE LAW, AND IN WHOM: (a) in the NOBILITY and the holders of estates, fear of losing seigneurial rights and labour services — and rightly so, because although § 16 abolished serfdom, THE ROBOT AND SUBJECTION REMAINED UNTIL 1848; (b) in the COURT AND THE POLICE, the fear that natural-law language is THE LANGUAGE OF REVOLUTION and could serve to derive political rights against the state — which is why it remains confined to private law and says nothing about the citizen's relation to power; (c) in the CHURCH, fear of secularization and of losing influence over marriage law; (d) and among conservatives generally, the fear that law would become detached from historically given conditions — which is exactly the reproach Thun will voice forty years later.

cards.q: What was the road to the ABGB in Austria?
cards.a: 1753 Maria Theresa sets up a COMPILATION COMMISSION → the CODEX THERESIANUS (1766), not adopted for its bulk and casuistry. 1781 THE ABOLITION OF SERFDOM. 1786 the JOSEPHINE CODE — only the first part (the law of persons). The commission is led by MARTINI, then ZEILLER (a Kantian). 1797 the WEST GALICIAN CODE as a trial run. On 1 June 1811 the ABGB is promulgated, in force from 1 January 1812, for the GERMAN HEREDITARY LANDS (not Hungary).

cards.q: What hopes were invested in § 16 ABGB?
cards.a: EQUALITY OF ALL BEFORE PRIVATE LAW regardless of estate and denomination; THE LEGAL PERSONALITY OF EVERY HUMAN BEING AS A PERSON, that is, the prohibition of treating a human being as a thing; the definitive END OF PERSONAL UNFREEDOM; and the idea that LAW CAN BE DERIVED FROM REASON and made universal. Background: the Enlightenment, Kant's autonomy (Zeiller was a Kantian), the abolition of serfdom.

cards.q: What fears did such a sentence in positive law arouse, and in whom?
cards.a: In the NOBILITY, fear of losing seigneurial rights — rightly so, because § 16 abolished serfdom but THE ROBOT AND SUBJECTION REMAINED UNTIL 1848. In the COURT AND THE POLICE, fear that natural-law language is THE LANGUAGE OF REVOLUTION and could be used to derive political rights — which is why it stays confined to private law. In the CHURCH, fear of the secularization of marriage law. And among conservatives, fear that law would become DETACHED FROM HISTORICALLY GIVEN CONDITIONS.

4.title: The legislator against the courts: from the ban on interpretation to § 7 ABGB
4.text: THE TENSION: the legislator wants his will applied exactly; the judge must decide even where the statute is silent or unclear — and thereby develops the law. The Enlightenment legislator distrusted this, and from experience: the French PARLEMENTS were pre-revolutionary courts that claimed the right to register (and thus block) royal acts and to interpret them in their own way, so that the judge was perceived as a rival for power. THE INSTRUMENT BY WHICH THE POWER OF THE COURTS WAS LIMITED IS THE BAN ON INTERPRETATION AND THE DUTY TO REFER: the judge was not allowed to interpret the statute and in case of doubt had to TURN TO THE LEGISLATOR for an authentic interpretation — in French the RÉFÉRÉ LÉGISLATIF (introduced in 1790), and similarly in Prussia with the ALR through a legislative commission. The premise was the idea of a GAPLESS CODE and of the judge as the 'MOUTH OF THE LAW' (Montesquieu: la bouche de la loi). WHAT THE ABGB DID WITH THIS — and this is the point of the question: IT ABANDONED IT. § 6 ABGB EXPRESSLY IMPOSES INTERPRETATION ON THE JUDGE: no meaning may be given to a statute other than that which follows from the proper meaning of the words in their context and from the clear intention of the legislator. And § 7 deals with gaps: where a case cannot be decided either from the words or from the natural meaning of the statute, REGARD IS HAD TO SIMILAR CASES (ANALOGY OF STATUTE), then to the grounds of other related statutes (ANALOGY OF LAW), and finally the case is decided ACCORDING TO THE NATURAL PRINCIPLES OF LAW (natürliche Rechtsgrundsätze), having regard to circumstances carefully ascertained. THAT IS A REMARKABLE ADMISSION: the code itself reckons with HAVING GAPS and entrusts the judge with filling them — and even by reference to natural law. THE DIFFERENCE FROM THE FRENCH TRADITION: (1) France introduced the référé législatif and forbade the judge to create general rules — ART. 5 OF THE CODE CIVIL to this day forbids deciding by way of a general provision (the ban on ARRÊTS DE RÈGLEMENT), so that a judgment binds only in its own case; (2) at the same time ART. 4 OF THE CODE CIVIL punishes DENEGATIO IUSTITIAE — a judge who refuses to decide on the ground of the silence, obscurity or insufficiency of the statute commits a denial of justice; the code therefore forces the judge to decide but will not concede that he is thereby making law. (3) The French conception remains EXEGETICAL (the 19th-century SCHOOL OF EXEGESIS: 'I know nothing of civil law, I teach the Code Napoléon'), whereas the Austrian one is more open from the outset and doctrine and case law have more room there. (4) The référé législatif proved unworkable in France and was abandoned in 1837 — practice took interpretation back.

terms.def: The judge's duty to turn to the legislator in case of doubt for an authentic interpretation; France 1790, abandoned 1837.

cards.q: By what instrument was the power of the courts limited, and why?
cards.a: BY THE BAN ON INTERPRETATION AND THE DUTY TO REFER — in case of doubt the judge had to TURN TO THE LEGISLATOR for an authentic interpretation (the RÉFÉRÉ LÉGISLATIF, France 1790; similarly with the Prussian ALR). The premise was the idea of a GAPLESS CODE and of the judge as the 'MOUTH OF THE LAW'. The distrust came from experience with the French PARLEMENTS, which blocked and reinterpreted royal acts.

cards.q: What did the ABGB do with it?
cards.a: IT ABANDONED IT. § 6 EXPRESSLY IMPOSES INTERPRETATION on the judge (the meaning of the words in context and the clear intention of the legislator). § 7 deals with gaps: first SIMILAR CASES (analogy of statute), then THE GROUNDS OF RELATED STATUTES (analogy of law), and finally THE NATURAL PRINCIPLES OF LAW. It is a remarkable admission: the code itself reckons with HAVING GAPS and entrusts the judge with filling them.

cards.q: How does the French tradition differ from the Austrian?
cards.a: ART. 5 OF THE CODE CIVIL to this day FORBIDS DECIDING BY WAY OF A GENERAL PROVISION (arrêts de règlement), while ART. 4 punishes DENEGATIO IUSTITIAE — the judge MUST decide, but the code will not concede that he is thereby making law. The French conception remains EXEGETICAL ('I know nothing of civil law, I teach the Code Napoléon'), the Austrian is more open. The référé législatif proved unworkable and was abandoned in 1837.

5.title: The Historical School of Law
5.text: ITS ORIGIN: Germany after 1814, in the atmosphere of the anti-Napoleonic upsurge and of Romanticism. The trigger is the DISPUTE ABOUT CODIFICATION: in 1814 A. F. J. THIBAUT publishes 'On the Necessity of a General Civil Law for Germany' and calls for a uniform German code on the French model; FRIEDRICH CARL VON SAVIGNY replies in the same year with 'ON THE VOCATION OF OUR AGE FOR LEGISLATION AND JURISPRUDENCE' and argues that THE AGE HAS NO SUCH VOCATION. THE ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE ENLIGHTENMENT CODIFICATIONS: (1) law CANNOT BE THOUGHT UP OUT OF REASON like mathematics — it is not a construction but an ORGANIC GROWTH; (2) a codification will FREEZE THE LAW at one moment and prevent its further growth; (3) German legal scholarship is NOT YET RIPE for it and lacks historical knowledge of its own law; (4) the universalist claim of rational natural law OVERLOOKS THE PARTICULARITY OF NATIONS; (5) and the existing codifications are, on their view, scientifically inadequate. WHAT LAW RESTS ON ACCORDING TO THEM: ON THE 'SPIRIT OF THE NATION' (VOLKSGEIST). Law arises like language and mores — SILENTLY, GRADUALLY, OUT OF THE INNER FORCE OF THE NATION, not from the will of a legislator; its true form is CUSTOM, and a statute is merely its record. THE METHODS: (1) HISTORICAL — the study of the sources in their own time, philological precision, editions of texts (hence the vast critical editions of sources); (2) SYSTEMATIC — the elaboration of concepts and their internal connections, that is, the building of a 'system'; the two are combined in Savigny's 'SYSTEM OF MODERN ROMAN LAW' (1840–49). The school splits into ROMANISTS (Savigny, Puchta, Windscheid — the law is sought in received Roman law) and GERMANISTS (Eichhorn, Beseler, Gierke — who seek it in Germanic sources and reproach the Romanists with calling a foreign law the national spirit). THE DRIVING FORCE OF LEGAL DEVELOPMENT IS, ON THEIR VIEW, LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP AND ITS BEARERS, THAT IS, THE LEARNED PROFESSION OF LAWYERS. That is a paradox worth remembering: LAW IS SUPPOSED TO GROW OUT OF THE SPIRIT OF THE NATION, BUT THE SPOKESMAN OF THAT SPIRIT IS A PROFESSOR OF LAW, NOT THE PEOPLE. From this it also follows that the school leads in the end to a codification after all: the Pandectism it produced gave the BGB (1900) its concepts and its system.

terms.def: The spirit of the nation — the source of law according to the Historical School; law arises like language and mores, silently and gradually.

cards.q: What did the Historical School of Law arise from, and what arguments did it have against codification?
cards.a: From the DISPUTE ABOUT CODIFICATION in 1814: THIBAUT calls for a uniform German code, SAVIGNY replies with 'ON THE VOCATION OF OUR AGE…' and argues that the age HAS NO SUCH VOCATION. The arguments: 1) law CANNOT BE THOUGHT UP OUT OF REASON, it is an ORGANIC GROWTH. 2) A codification will FREEZE THE LAW. 3) Scholarship is NOT YET RIPE. 4) Universalism OVERLOOKS THE PARTICULARITY OF NATIONS.

cards.q: What does law rest on according to the Historical School, and by what methods did it work?
cards.a: On the 'SPIRIT OF THE NATION' (VOLKSGEIST) — law arises like language and mores, SILENTLY AND GRADUALLY, and its true form is CUSTOM. The methods: the HISTORICAL (the study of sources in their own time, philological precision, critical editions) and the SYSTEMATIC (the building of concepts and their connections) — the two combined in Savigny's 'System of Modern Roman Law' (1840–49). It splits into ROMANISTS (Savigny, Puchta, Windscheid) and GERMANISTS (Eichhorn, Beseler, Gierke).

cards.q: Who is the driving force of legal development according to the Historical School, and where is the paradox?
cards.a: LEGAL SCHOLARSHIP AND THE LEARNED PROFESSION OF LAWYERS. The paradox: LAW IS SUPPOSED TO GROW OUT OF THE SPIRIT OF THE NATION, BUT THE SPOKESMAN OF THAT SPIRIT IS A PROFESSOR OF LAW, NOT THE PEOPLE. And the school leads in the end to a codification after all — the Pandectism it produced gave the BGB (1900) its concepts and its system.

6.title: Source: Thun's speech of 11 May 1852
6.text: THE SOURCE: 'The General Civil Code, rightly the most celebrated legal compendium of recent times, is not, like every human work, free of defects. It grew out of the philosophical school then almost universally prevailing, beyond which, however, scholarship has since advanced; out of a school which DID NOT REGARD CIVIL LAW AS AN ORDER FOUNDED ON HIGHER MORAL LAWS AND ON HISTORICALLY GIVEN ACTUAL CONDITIONS, but as a PRODUCT OF THE SPECULATION OF HUMAN REASON. This view DETACHED AUSTRIAN JURISPRUDENCE FROM ITS HISTORICAL FOUNDATIONS.' HOW AND ON WHAT BASIS THE ABGB IS CRITICIZED: not for individual provisions but FOR ITS PHILOSOPHICAL FOUNDATION. It is reproached with having grown out of RATIONAL NATURAL LAW, that is, out of 'the speculation of human reason', and with therefore lacking a twofold anchorage — in a MORAL ORDER (meaning a Christian one) and in HISTORICALLY GIVEN CONDITIONS. The criticism is therefore made from the position of the HISTORICAL SCHOOL OF LAW, and in its conservative, Catholic-tinged version. THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: LEO THUN-HOHENSTEIN was minister of religion and education from 1849 to 1860, that is, in the period of NEO-ABSOLUTISM after the defeat of the 1848 revolution and after the Sylvester Patents (1851), which abolished the constitution and fundamental rights. Thun carried out a fundamental REFORM OF THE UNIVERSITIES (freedom of scholarship and teaching on the German model, habilitation, seminars) and at the same time a RESTRUCTURING OF LEGAL STUDY: he strengthened the historical subjects — Roman law, German and Austrian legal history, canon law — at the expense of natural law, which practically disappeared from the curriculum. His speech of 1852 is the programmatic justification of precisely that change. THE AUTHOR'S CONCEPTION OF LAW: law is NOT A CREATION OF REASON but an ORDER GIVEN FROM WITHOUT — by a higher moral law (and hence ultimately by religion) and by history. The legislator is to find and develop it, not to construct it. Legal scholarship must therefore be HISTORICAL, not speculative, and the lawyer must be educated in the history of his law. AN IRONY WORTH MENTIONING: Thun's reform of study was indisputably modernizing and gave Austria legal history of a European scholarly standard — but its motive was restorative, namely to remove from the curriculum the natural-law language with which one could argue against power.

cards.q: How and from what position does Thun criticize the ABGB?
cards.a: Not for individual provisions but FOR ITS PHILOSOPHICAL FOUNDATION: it grew out of RATIONAL NATURAL LAW, that is, out of 'THE SPECULATION OF HUMAN REASON', and therefore lacks an anchorage in a MORAL ORDER and in HISTORICALLY GIVEN CONDITIONS — it 'detached Austrian jurisprudence from its historical foundations'. The criticism is made from the position of the HISTORICAL SCHOOL OF LAW in its conservative, Catholic-tinged version.

cards.q: What is the historical context of Thun's speech and what did Thun do?
cards.a: LEO THUN-HOHENSTEIN was minister of religion and education 1849–1860, that is, under NEO-ABSOLUTISM after the defeat of the 1848 revolution and the Sylvester Patents (1851). He carried out a REFORM OF THE UNIVERSITIES (freedom of scholarship and teaching, habilitation, seminars) and a RESTRUCTURING OF LEGAL STUDY: he strengthened the HISTORICAL SUBJECTS (Roman law, legal history, canon law) AT THE EXPENSE OF NATURAL LAW, which practically disappeared.

cards.a: Law is NOT A CREATION OF REASON but an ORDER GIVEN FROM WITHOUT — by a higher moral law and by history; the legislator is to FIND AND DEVELOP it, not construct it, and scholarship must be HISTORICAL. THE IRONY: the reform of study was indisputably MODERNIZING and gave Austria legal history of a European standard — but its MOTIVE WAS RESTORATIVE, namely to remove from the curriculum the natural-law language with which one could argue against power.
